key_facts: Ofgem is expected to announce a new domestic energy price cap that will take effect in January, with a typical annual bill forecast by Cornwall Insight to rise by 26%.

Cornwall Insight's forecast implies a typical household bill increase of about £37 a month from January to end of March, or about £443 a year (to £2,166) compared with the current cap; the source notes actual usage varies.

Wholesale gas prices are the dominant driver, with the average gas price reported 166% higher than late last year, before the Iran war began, according to Energy UK; storage levels are relatively low ahead of winter.

The government will make a £100 support payment to millions of households (automatically to council tax bands A–D in England, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales), a temporary 5% VAT cut on electricity until end of June next year (expected to save a typical household about £45 a year), and a £150 Warm Home Discount for six million benefit-receiving households this winter.
importance_reason: Regulated domestic price-cap change affecting about 20 million households, with a wider consumer-spending effect; not a central-bank or market-shock event.
market_link: Higher gas prices and a rising energy-debt backdrop may weigh on household spending and UK consumer demand; the source describes this as a knock-on effect on the wider economy.

key_facts: Energy bills are to soar in January as the Ofgem energy price cap rises at the coldest time of the year; the cap affects over 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by Ofgem every three months.

The increase is driven mainly by higher wholesale gas prices, which the source attributes to the US-Israel war with Iran; the government temporarily removed VAT from domestic electricity bills, cutting about £45 a year from a typical bill, and millions of households will receive an automatic £100 payment to help with winter costs.

Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers will be 54.83p a day for electricity (lower than the previous period) and 29.68p a day for gas (largely unchanged); the government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges without published details.

From April 2026, grid-investment charges of about £6 a month for a typical household started to appear on bills, as part of a £28bn Ofgem-approved grid upgrade adding up to £108 to bills by 2031; the Energy Company Obligation charges were scrapped from 1 April and renewable projects are 75% funded from general taxation for three years.
importance_reason: Regulated price cap change affecting over 20 million UK households during a winter price rise, driven by a geopolitical energy shock.
market_link: Higher UK wholesale gas prices linked to the Iran conflict feed directly into the Ofgem cap, with knock-on effects for gas-sensitive sectors and UK inflation expectations.

region: US / global (China, EU, Mexico, Japan and 16 jurisdictions in total)
key_facts: The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on several countries, per BBC understanding; 16 jurisdictions are affected, including China, the European Union, Mexico and Japan.
The move follows a Section 301 investigation launched in March, after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's Liberation Day tariffs illegal; those earlier tariffs were first announced in April 2025.
Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on deals previously struck with Trump; an interim US-China agreement is set to expire on 10 January.
China extended the suspension of a ban on exports of critical minerals including gallium, germanium and antimony until 27 January; the ban would otherwise have taken effect on Friday.
importance_reason: Broad new tariff action covering 16 major trading jurisdictions, with rising US-China tension and an expiring interim trade deal.
market_link: New import tariffs and possible escalation in US-China trade friction could affect trade flows, commodity and critical-mineral supply, and currencies and equities of exposed economies.

key_facts: Licence-free micro-cars (motorised quadricycles, max 45 km/h, banned on motorways) are growing in Europe: in France, registrations rose from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year; European sales went from 30,000 to 60,000 over the past five years.

Minimum driving age for these cars is 14 in France and Italy (with a road safety certificate and eight hours of training), 15 in Germany and Spain, and 16 in the UK. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric, and teenagers account for a quarter of mini-car sales (Citroën Ami, launched 2020); the market was also shifting after EU rules made mopeds costly for manufacturers.

Aixam has invested €30m in expanding French production capacity; sales are growing in other European countries even as the French market slows, which the article links to the withdrawal of electric-model subsidies in France.
